The 56 member countries of the Commonwealth, including Canada, celebrate Commonwealth Day every year on the second Monday in March. It is a day of observance by more than 2 billion citizens of their common bonds and the contribution of the Commonwealth to the creation of a harmonious global environment. Canada has been a monarchy for centuries - first under the kings of France in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, then under the British Crown in the 18th and 19th centuries, and now as a kingdom in her own right.
KLICK: A klick is a military term used to denote a distance of one kilometre. It is commonly used in Canada when referring to distance or speed.
KNOLL: Knolls are found throughout Canada, and the term generally refers to small, rounded hills or mounds that often create scenic viewpoints or unique natural features in the landscape. Knolls are a common geographical feature, especially in hilly or mountainous regions, and are present in various places across the country. High Knoll in Minnekhada Regional Park near Coquitlam, British Columbia, is a popular hiking destination with impressive views. Additionally, knoll-like formations appear in areas across Alberta and Ontario, adding character to the natural landscape and offering vantage points in parks and along hiking trails. Knolls can also be found in more northern areas of Canada where glacial activity historically shaped the terrain, leaving behind knolls, drumlins, and other geological features.
LABEL: More than ever, Canadians are looking to the label to guide their choices. Amid rising trade tensions and growing national pride, more shoppers are seeking out goods labelled “Made in Canada” and “Product of Canada.” A recent survey found that 84% of Canadians check labels to see where items are made, and 77% say they’ll choose Canadian – even if it costs more. That little label is a symbol of pride, connecting Canadians to the people and places behind every product.
LAGER: The top selling style of beer in Canada is, by far, the pale lager. December 10th is National Lager Day in Canada!
LAKER: Lakers are massive freighters built to carry bulk Canadian cargo, including grain, iron ore, salt, and limestone. Since the late 19th century, they have hauled raw materials from docks in the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Seaway to the industrial centres of Ontario and Quebec. Many lakers are specially designed with narrow beams and long hulls to fit the waterways’ locks and channels, making them unique to Canada’s inland shipping routes.
LAKES: Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined! Almost 9% of Canada's total surface area is covered by freshwater.
LAMPS: Thomas Leopold "Carbide" Willson (March 14, 1860 – December 20, 1915) was a Canadian inventor. He was born on a farm near Princeton, Canada West, in 1860 and went to school in Hamilton, Ontario. By the age of 21, he had designed and patented the first electric arc lamps used in Hamilton. Willson's accidental discovery of calcium carbide in 1892 led to widespread use of carbide lamps in early cars and motorcycles and as headlamps for miners.
LANES: Did you know that 5-pin bowling was invented in 1909 by Canadian Thomas F. Ryan in Toronto? Bowling alleys have a rich history in Canada. Hamilton's [Skyway Bowl](https://www.skywaybowl.com/) is home to City 10-pin - the oldest bowling league on the planet that has been rolling for over 120 years! Since opening in 1930, [Commodore Lanes & Billiards](https://www.commodorelanes.ca/) in Vancouver is one of Canada's oldest surviving recreation centres. [Steelheads and Strikes](https://www.steelheadsandstrikes.com/) in Arnprior is the oldest, continually operating bowling alley in the country, with the original lanes dating back to the 1930 as well. If you can spare some time to play, go hit the lanes and give bowling a try...it may be right up your alley!
LARCH: Larches are among the dominant plants in the boreal forests of Canada. Larches are the only Canadian deciduous conifers, turning golden and shedding all their leaves in fall.
LATKE: Latkes are crispy and golden potato pancakes that are a cherished part of Jewish cuisine and culture. While they’re famously associated with Hanukkah, these delicious treats are enjoyed year-round in Jewish households and beyond. This beloved dish is especially meaningful during [Canadian Jewish Heritage Month](https://jewishheritage.ca/), celebrated every May since 2018. Canada's Jewish population, the fourth largest in the world, has made incredible contributions to our country in areas like arts, science, and social justice. Celebrating Jewish heritage – and enjoying cultural dishes like latkes – is a delicious way to honour the diversity and traditions that enrich Canada.
LAYER: Nanaimo Bars are a Canadian dessert staple originating in Nanaimo, a city on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. It consists of three layers: a graham wafer crumb and shredded coconut base, a custard-flavoured butter icing filling, and a chocolate ganache topping. The Nanaimo bar was popularized nationwide after being highlighted as a classic Canadian dessert at Expo 86. In 2006, the Nanaimo bar was declared Canada’s favourite confection by a reader’s poll in the National Post.
LEARN: October 5 is World Teachers’ Day, a time to celebrate the educators who inspire students to learn and grow. Across Canada, more than 500,000 teachers bring creativity, dedication, and heart into their classrooms each day. Their efforts are a big reason why Canada is recognized for its strong public education system, consistently ranking among the best in the world. Thank you to all the teachers who make a difference every day!
LEMON: One of the greatest mysteries of the Canadian Rockies is the legend of the so-called “Lost Lemon Mine.” The Lost Lemon Mine is a legendary gold deposit reputedly somewhere between the Crowsnest Pass and the Highwood River in southwestern Alberta, discovered about 1870 by prospectors Frank Lemon and "Blackjack." Thousands have since searched for the fabulous lode; many have died mysteriously. Check out Craig Baird's [Canadian History Ehx podcast](https://canadaehx.com/2023/06/02/the-lost-lemon-mine/) to learn more!
LILAC: Lilacs are a spring flower and you can find these in gardens across Canada, but the small village of Franktown, Ontario, part of the township of Beckwith, is special as it is known as the Lilac Capital of Ontario. This Lanark County township near Ottawa is famous for its country road called Lilac Lane bordered by beautiful, fragrant lilac bushes, and is home to an annual Lilac Festival every May. If you love gardens, add the Franktown Lilac Festival to your travel list.
LINGO: Before Canuckle brought daily word fun to Canadians, there was Lingo – the classic word game show that combined luck, logic, and quick thinking! Produced in Vancouver and originally airing in the late 1980s, Lingo featured contestants guessing five-letter words to fill a bingo-style grid, with each correct guess bringing them closer to a winning line. A Canadian version later aired in the late 1990s, hosted by Paul Houde, introducing a new generation to the fun of wordplay. Decades later, Canadians are still hooked on guessing words – proving that a love for lingo never goes out of style!
LIONS: The [Canadian Football League](https://www.cfl.ca/) season is underway! The [BC Lions](https://www.bclions.com/) are a professional Canadian football team based in Vancouver, British Columbia. The Lions played their first season in 1954, and have played every season since, making them the oldest professional sports franchise in British Columbia. They have appeared in the league's Grey Cup championship game 10 times, winning six, with their most recent championship occurring in 2011. The team is named for the Lions, a pair of mountain peaks overlooking the team's home city of Vancouver.
LODGE: A beaver home is called a lodge. Beavers live in wetland habitats along lakes and rivers and are some of the best architects in the wild. Some even call them the original Canadian lumberjacks!
LOGIC: Happy Star Trek Day! In the Star Trek universe, Vulcans are an extraterrestrial humanoid species known as logical beings who have removed emotions from their daily lives. The official Star Trek Capital of Canada is Vulcan, Alberta. The town even has a prominent display of a Starship Enterprise statue. Live long and prosper! 🖖
LOONS: Loons have beautiful, crimson red eyes, but this is only during mating season.
LOTTO: Canada's [Pollard Banknote](https://www.pollardbanknote.com/), headquartered in Winnipeg, plays a major role in the world of lotteries! This Canadian company has been a leader in producing instant lotto tickets for decades, supplying games to lottery corporations around the world. Pollard Banknote is responsible for printing roughly 85 per cent of the scratch-and-win lottery tickets sold in Canada. It's also the second-largest printer of those products in the world! From scratch-off tickets to digital lottery options, Pollard Banknote brings a bit of Canadian creativity and security to lotto experiences far and wide. From coast to coast, chances are, the next scratch ticket you buy has a bit of Canadian innovation behind it.
LOYAL: June 6 marks the 81st anniversary of [D-Day and the Battle of Normandy](https://veterans.gc.ca/en/remembrance/wars-and-conflicts/second-world-war/d-day-and-the-battle-of-normandy). On D-Day – June 6, 1944 – Canada showed the world what it means to be loyal. Over 14,000 Canadian troops landed on Juno Beach, fighting with unwavering dedication alongside Allied forces. Their loyalty to freedom, to each other, and to the mission remained steadfast even under relentless fire – a testament to the loyal spirit that defined Canada's role in the war and its lasting legacy in the fight for peace.
LUCKY: Whenever Canada needs a bit of good fortune at the Olympic Games, you can count on a lucky loonie to come through. The tradition was started in 2002 at the Salt Lake City Olympics when Canadian icemaker Trent Evans snuck a loonie underneath centre ice when needing a marker for the faceoff dot. Evans left the loonie there as a good luck charm for the Canadians, and it worked beautifully, with Canada winning gold in both men's and women's hockey for the first time.
LUMEN: [Winterlude](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/winterlude.html) is underway in Ottawa and Gatineau, and this year's festivities feature [Lumen Eira](https://limbicmedia.ca/projects/lumen-eira-night-walk/) - a mesmorizing illumination experience animating Confederation Park. This dazzling display blends light and sound, transforming the park into a winter wonderland after dark. Trees glow and pulse with colours synchronized to custom soundscapes, inspired by nature and imagination. Let the interplay of light, sound, and winter's magic draw you into a world where reality is suspended, and imagination takes centre stage!
LUPIN: Lupins are iconic tall-stalked flowers found across Canada, blooming in shades of purple, pink, blue and white from late June to July. Lupin flowers are hardy perennials, able to survive even the coldest winter temperatures in Canada. Their deep roots and seeds endure frost and snow, ready to sprout vibrant spikes of colour when spring arrives. Lupins also enrich the soil with their nitrogen-fixing properties, making them resilient and valuable in Canadian gardens and wild landscapes.
MACRO: In economics, macro means looking at the big picture – growth, innovation, and how whole economies thrive. Canadian economist Peter Howitt shared the [2025 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/howitt/facts/) for groundbreaking research showing how new ideas drive long-term growth. His work in macroeconomics helped the world understand how innovation fuels prosperity – a truly big-picture contribution from a brilliant Canadian mind!
MAGIC: The [International Brotherhood of Magicians](https://www.magician.org/) (I.B.M.) is an organization for both professional and amateur close-up and stage magicians, with approximately 15,000 members worldwide. It was founded in Winnipeg, Manitoba in 1922, and is now the largest organization of magicians in the world. Winnipeg was also home to one of Canada's most famous magicians, Doug Henning, who had a storied career around the world. He retired in the mid-1980s, selling some of his most famous illusions to another famous magician, David Copperfield.
MAIZE: Did you know that maize, or corn, is one of Canada's most important crops? It thrives particularly in Ontario and Quebec, where it’s often used for animal feed, as well as human consumption in products like corn syrup and popcorn. As Halloween approaches, corn becomes a festive staple, with many Canadians decorating their homes with corn husks and using maize to create seasonal decorations like cornucopias or even haunted corn mazes. These maize mazes offer a fun way for families to celebrate the spooky season while appreciating the agricultural heritage of Canada.
MANGA: Manga, the Japanese style of comics and graphic novels, has a growing fanbase across Canada. Readers enjoy a wide range of genres, from action-packed adventures to heartwarming slice-of-life stories. Canadian artists are creating their own manga-inspired works, and conventions like Anime North and Ottawa Comiccon celebrate this art form, showing how Canada embraces global storytelling and visual creativity. Michael Nicoll Yahgulanaas, a Haida artist, has blended Indigenous storytelling with manga aesthetics, creating works like Red: A Haida Manga.
MANOR: [Escape Manor](https://www.escapemanor.com/) is known for its interactive and immersive escape rooms in Ottawa, but on September 10, 2017, they organized the world's largest scavenger hunt consisting of 2,732 people! Participants took part in the scavenger hunt in celebration of Canada's 150th anniversary and attempted to complete as many of the 150 tasks as they could throughout the city of Ottawa. Canada now holds the Guinness World Record for the largest scavenger hunt thanks to Escape Manor!
MAPLE: The maple leaf is one of the most recognizable symbols of Canada and is featured on the national flag.
MARSH: Canada's wetlands are diverse. They take the form of marshes, bogs, fens, swamps and open water. They appear on the prairies, in the boreal forest, along coastlines and even in the tundra. Marshes are treeless wetlands with an abundance of herbaceous plants, including grasses, sedges, reeds and cattails. They are highly productive ecosystems teeming with life. The marsh at Point Pelee National Park in southern Ontario supports 19 species at risk and is a critical stop-over for migratory birds, which rely on the chance to forage for food in the marsh after a long flight.
MASKS: Today marks the start of the 2023-24 National Hockey League Season! The goaltender mask is now a mandatory piece of equipment, but that wasn't always the case. The first goaltender to wear a mask in any level of organized ice hockey was Elizabeth Graham of Queen’s University in 1927 who wore a fencing mask. The first NHL goalie to wear a mask full-time was Jacques Plante of the Montreal Canadiens. During the 1959 season, Plante wore a face-hugging fibreglass mask created by Bill Burchmore, a children’s hockey coach and Canadiens fan who worked at Fiberglas Canada in Montreal. Goalie masks have certainly come a long way since then!
MAYBE: "Call Me Maybe" is a song by Canadian singer-songwriter [Carly Rae Jepsen](https://www.carlyraemusic.com/). The song was the best-selling single worldwide in 2012, selling over 12 million copies in that year alone. "Call Me Maybe" reached number one in more than 19 countries, and Jepsen received the 2013 Juno Award for Best Single of the Year. The song is also the seventh best-selling digital single of all time.
MEATY: If you are looking for hearty comfort food, look no further than French Canadian Tourtière, a meaty, flavourful pie that is typically enjoyed around the holidays (but is also enjoyed all year long). The tourtiere is a traditional Quebecois spiced meat pie, and the ground or chopped filling usually includes pork and is sometimes mixed with other meats, including local game, such as rabbit, pheasant, or moose. Tourtière is the quintessential Canadian comfort food that has a worldwide appeal!
MEDIC: Jennie Trout became Canada’s first licensed female physician in 1875 when she received her medical licence from the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario. As a trailblazing medic, she challenged 19th-century norms and opened doors for women in medicine. Trout went on to establish a successful practice in Toronto, inspiring countless women to follow in her footsteps. Her legacy remains a milestone in Canadian healthcare history.
MERRY: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! Across Canada, "Merry Christmas" rings out as part of holiday traditions from coast to coast. While customs vary by region, the season brings a shared spirit of joy and warmth throughout the country. Canadians celebrate with everything from festive parades to bustling holiday markets, gathering with family, friends, and neighbours to make the season special. Whether it's around a Christmas tree, at an outdoor rink, or in a snowy winter wonderland, Canada's holiday spirit is as bright and cheerful as the greeting itself!
METAL: In 2021, Canada produced over 60 minerals and metals worth $44 billion. Canadian mines produced 223 tonnes of gold in 2021, ranking Canada as the fourth-largest global producer of the precious metal. Canada is a leading global producer of many critical minerals including those used in advanced battery technologies, such as cobalt, graphite and nickel, and is the world's fourth-largest producer of primary aluminum.
METIS: The Métis invented the york boat, used by the Hudson's Bay Company to carry furs and trade goods along waterways.
METRO: Metro systems help move millions of Canadians every day, with rapid transit networks operating in cities like Toronto, Montréal, Vancouver, and Edmonton. [Canada’s first true metro](https://www.stm.info/en/info/networks/metro) opened in Montréal in 1966, designed with rubber-tired trains to allow for quieter rides and steeper grades. Even during heavy snowfall, these systems are built to keep commuters moving and cities connected year-round.
MOGUL: Canadian moguls skiers have won an impressive 9 Olympic medals over the years! Medallists include Jean-Luc Brassard, Jennifer Heil, Alexandre Bilodeau, sisters Justine & Chloé Dufour-Lapointe, and Mikaël Kingsbury. Bilodeau won a gold medal in the men's moguls at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, becoming the first Canadian to win a gold medal at an Olympic Games held in Canada.
MOIST: [Moist](https://moistonline.com/) is a Canadian rock band that formed in 1992. They released three studio albums in the 1990s, becoming a staple of Canadian rock music. The band, led by frontman David Usher, became a staple of the Canadian alternative rock scene in the 1990s. Moist has been nominated for ten Juno Awards, winning two, including Best New Group at the 1995 Juno Awards.
MOOSE: The moose is the largest species of deer in the world. The average weight of a fully grown male moose (a bull) is 1500 lbs!
MORNE: [Gros Morne National Park](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/nl/grosmorne) is a breathtaking landscape on Newfoundland and Labrador's west coast! Its name means "big gloomy" in French, but there's nothing dreary about this stunning UNESCO World Heritage Site. The park is home to towering fjords, ancient mountains, and the Tablelands - a rare landscape where the Earth's mantle is exposed! Adventurous hikers can take on Gros Morne Mountain, where the reward is an unforgettable view stretching for kilometres.
MOUNT: Canada is home to some impressive mountain peaks, but Mount Logan tops them all at 5956m high. It is part of the St. Elias Mountains in the Kluane National Park and Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Canada's Yukon Territory is home to 8 of Canada's tallest mountains, including Mount Logan.
MOUNTIE: The Mountie is one of Canada's most iconic symbols. Short for “Royal Canadian Mounted Police” (RCMP), Mounties have served as Canada’s national police force since 1873. Originally created to bring law and order to the western territories, the RCMP became known for their striking red serge uniforms, wide-brimmed Stetson hats, and steadfast motto: Maintiens le droit (“Uphold the right”). Today, Mounties serve communities across the country—and around the world—as ambassadors of Canadian service, tradition, and pride.
MUNCH: One of Canada's most nostalgic snack brands has made a triumphant return, 20 years after disappearing from shelves. Munchies, the Hostess chips beloved by those who grew up in the '80s and '90s, are back, along with their iconic characters - Red, Yellow, and Orange. Canadians are sure to be munching on these tasty treats once again, savouring the familiar crunch and a taste of the past!
NAMES: In 1995, Brent Peterson & Margot Newton, an expectant Toronto couple, combed through thousands of baby names trying to agree on just one. Their debate inspired them to invent [Namesake](https://www.namesakegame.com/), a homegrown Canadian board game where players pair up famous people who share the same first name. Thirty years later, Namesake has been reborn as a free daily web puzzle. Try it for yourself at [namesakegame.com](https://www.namesakegame.com/)!
NATAL: In Nova Scotia, Natal Day is celebrated on the first Monday in August and marks the "birth" of the Halifax–Dartmouth area. The name comes from the Latin natalis, meaning birth – fitting for a holiday that honours the founding of Halifax in 1749 and the growth of neighbouring communities. First celebrated in 1895, Natal Day has grown into a beloved long weekend tradition filled with parades, fireworks, concerts, and one of Canada’s oldest road races. It’s a joyful celebration of Nova Scotia’s history and coastal spirit!
NAVAL: There are 24 naval reserve divisions across Canada, including 4100+ citizen sailors strong. The Naval Reserve has played a critical role in Canada's safety and security. 2023 marks the 100th anniversary and 100 years of service to Canada! Thank you to all the brave sailors that serve and protect our country. Happy Centennial! #WeTheNavy #NavRes100
NECKS: The [Calgary Roughnecks](https://calgaryroughnecks.com/) are a professional box lacrosse team based in Calgary, Alberta. They are members of the Western Conference of the [National Lacrosse League](https://www.nll.com/) (NLL). The Roughnecks were founded in 2001, and have won the NLL Cup three times with the most recent being in 2019. The Roughnecks are one of five Canadian teams currently in the NLL, with a sixth Canadian team ([Ottawa Black Bears](https://www.nll.com/news/national-lacrosse-league-announces-the-launch-of-the-ottawa-black-bears-franchise/)) joining for the 2024-25 season.
NERVE: Canadian neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield helped pioneer the “Montreal procedure” to treat severe epilepsy while patients remained awake. By stimulating different areas of the brain, he could trace nerve responses and map the brain’s sensory regions. Famously, his first patient reported smelling burnt toast during the procedure, helping doctors pinpoint the source of her seizures. Penfield’s groundbreaking work at the [Montreal Neurological Institute](https://www.mcgill.ca/neuro/) transformed our understanding of how the brain and nervous system work.
NEVER: Never Cry Wolf by Canadian author Farley Mowat is a landmark work of Canadian nature writing that follows his time studying Arctic wolves in the North. First published in 1963, the book challenged widespread fears about wolves and helped shift public perception toward understanding and conservation. Blending observation, storytelling, and humour, it remains one of Canada’s most influential wilderness narratives.
NINTH: Did you know that the border between Canada and the United States along the 49th parallel is the longest undefended international boundary in the world? Stretching over 8,891 kilometres, the 49th parallel serves as the dividing line between the two countries for much of their shared border. The bi-national International Boundary Commission deals with matters relating to marking and maintaining the boundary, and the International Joint Commission deals with issues concerning boundary waters.
NOBLE: Today, Canada marks the Coronation of its new monarch, His Majesty King Charles III, beginning a new chapter in our country's history. In recognition of the RCMP's 150th anniversary and the Coronation, the King was officially presented with RCMP Musical Ride horse "Noble". The King has shared a personal connection to the RCMP as their Honorary Commissioner since 2012, and on Friday he was officially appointed Commissioner-in-Chief of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
NOISE: Happy National Acadian Day! Tintamarre is an Acadian tradition of marching through one's community making noise with improvised instruments and other noisemakers. The term originates from the Acadian French word meaning "clangour" or "din" meaning noise. The practice is intended to demonstrate the vitality and solidarity of Acadian society, and to express their pride in their Acadian heritage.
NORDIC: Nordic climates are defined by long, cold winters – something much of Canada knows well, with average February temperatures below freezing across most of the country. Those conditions have helped shape Canada’s strength in Nordic sports like cross-country skiing, ski jumping, biathlon, and Nordic combined, where athletes train for endurance, precision, and resilience in the cold. With the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milano–Cortina starting on February 6, many of Canada’s Nordic athletes will once again put those winter-hardened skills to the test on the world stage.
OCEAN: With marine waters spanning its west, north, and east coasts, Canada is an ocean nation. Canadians are influenced in many ways by the Pacific, Arctic, and Atlantic Oceans. Celebrate World Oceans Day on June 8th!
OPERA: World Opera Day is celebrated each year October 25th. It raises awareness for the positive impact and value of opera for society. Throughout the 20th century, great operatic singers have populated Canada’s cultural landscape - from Raoul Jobin, Portia White, Maureen Forrester and Jon Vickers to Gerald Finley, Rihab Chaieb, Rebecca Cuddy and Measha Brueggergosman. Over the years, opera singers from Canada have made Canadians proud on stages around the world! Learn more about the Canadian Opera Company at [coc.ca](https://www.coc.ca/).
OPTIC: Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light, letting information travel vast distances at incredible speeds. In Canada, optic-based networks expand internet access to rural, remote, and northern communities, connecting them to essential services. As more fibre reaches farther corners of the country, optical technology continues to play a quiet but powerful role in helping Canadians stay connected, no matter where they live.
ORBIT: The Manitoba government launched the Orbit program in 1965, which saw unique fibreglass sphere trashcans placed along the province's highways in an effort to reduce the amount of litter. The program lasted roughly till the 1990s across Manitoba highways.
ORGAN: Canadian Joseph Casavant was a world-renowned organ maker. In 1840, he produced his first church organ in his shop at Saint-Hyacinthe. When he retired in 1866, Casavant organs were in demand throughout eastern Canada. Under the direction of his sons, Claver and Samuel, the firm Casavant Frères acquired an international reputation as builders of fine instruments. Casavant Frères continues to build internationally recognized pipe organs for churches, concert halls, religious communities and teaching institutions.
OVENS: [Ovens Natural Park](https://www.ovenspark.com/) is a privately owned 180-acre pristine reserve of coastal forest, located on the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, along the scenic Lighthouse Route near Lunenburg. For hundreds of years, people have been drawn to the incredible beauty, diverse geography, fascinating history, and spiritual solace that make The Ovens Natural Park so unique. Every year, thousands of park visitors hike the spectacular trails along the cliffs to view the famous sea caves, or "Ovens" for which the park was named.
OWNED: Across Canada, many beloved businesses are family owned and operated, with traditions and know-how passed down through generations. From corner stores and hardware shops to local cafés and diners, these family-run enterprises are deeply rooted in the communities they serve. Built on trust, pride, and a personal touch, they continue to play a vital role in Canada’s economy and daily life.
OWNER: Happy [Canadian Innovation Week](https://canadianinnovationspace.ca/about/)! Business owners are the backbone of the Canadian economy, with small and medium-sized enterprises making up a whopping 99.8% of all businesses in the country. From local coffee shop owners to cutting-edge tech start-ups, these entrepreneurs drive growth and spark innovation across the nation. With their strong entrepreneurial spirit, Canadian business owners are fuelling progress, creating jobs, and helping communities thrive from coast to coast to coast.
OZONE: September 16 is [World Ozone Day](https://www.un.org/en/observances/ozone-day)! Canada is known for its commitment to environmental conservation, including efforts to protect the ozone layer through initiatives such as the [Montreal Protocol](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/corporate/international-affairs/partnerships-organizations/ozone-layer-depletion-montreal-convention.html). The Montreal Protocol has succeeded in halting the damage to the ozone layer and is helping the world in the battle against climate change. In Canada and around the world, the Montreal Protocol regulates the production and consumption of numerous substances that deplete the ozone layer, the Earth’s atmospheric shield that prevents UV radiation from harming humans and other forms of life. It is considered one of the most successful, global environmental agreements of all time.
PASTE: In 1884, Canadian chemist and pharmacist Marcellus Gilmore Edson received a patent for the manufacture of a peanut paste, which he named “peanut-candy.” Edson's patent for peanut-candy has been recognized as a forerunner to the commercially available peanut butter or spread.
PEAKS: Canada’s Yukon Territory is home to 8 of Canada’s tallest mountains, with Mount Logan topping them all at 5956m high. BC’s Snow Dome peak is a unique “three-ocean peak”, where if you poured a cup of water at the summit, the water could flow into the Pacific Ocean to the west, the Arctic Ocean to the north, or the Atlantic Ocean to the east.
PEAMEAL: Peameal is a traditional Canadian style of cured pork loin, often known as Canadian back bacon. It is rolled in cornmeal, giving it its signature golden coating and helping preserve the meat. Today, it is closely associated with Toronto food culture at the historic St. Lawrence Market, where it is a staple known for its savoury flavour and tender texture.
PEDAL: Pedal power takes over the streets of Ottawa each spring during the [CN Cycle for CHEO](https://cncycle.cheofoundation.com/). Held this year on Sunday, May 3, the event invites thousands of participants of all ages and skill levels to pedal, walk, or roll along scenic, car-free routes in support of the CHEO Foundation. Since its launch, the event has raised millions of dollars to help deliver life-saving care for children and youth across eastern Ontario.
PEELS: Today is Curling Day in Canada! From coast to coast to coast, Canadians celebrate the strategy, skill, and teamwork that make curling so special. One of the game’s most thrilling shots is the peel – a high-speed takeout designed to remove an opponent’s guard or stone, while sending the delivered stone out of play. Often used to clear the front of the house, the peel is essential for reducing your opponent’s scoring opportunities and shows off skill, timing, and strategy on the ice. Catch exciting shots and perfect peels at the 2026 Scotties in Mississauga, Ontario, as the best teams in Canada compete for the national women’s curling championship!
PELTS: Beaver pelts were an integral part of the early Canadian fur trade economy. The fur trade began in the 1600s in what is now Canada. It continued for more than 250 years. Beaver pelts were among the most sought-after furs due to the popularity of beaver top hats in Europe at the time. While the hunting of beavers was only a small part of life for Indigenous peoples before Europeans came, it soon became the predominant activity in some territories.
PEONY: Peonies are a beloved flower in Canadian gardens, known for their vibrant blooms and resilience to our northern climate. The [Canadian Peony Society](https://peony.ca/), established in 1998, is dedicated to the cultivation and appreciation of these beautiful flowers. Peonies are often seen as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune in many cultures, and their lush blossoms make them a popular choice for Canadian gardens. With over 30 species of peonies found worldwide, they thrive in Canada's diverse climates from coast to coast!
PERSON: On October 18, 1929, Canadian women officially became recognized as “persons” under the law — a landmark victory for equality. This moment, now celebrated as Persons Day, was the result of tireless advocacy by five remarkable women known as the Famous Five: Emily Murphy, Nellie McClung, Irene Parlby, Louise McKinney, and Henrietta Muir Edwards. Their achievement opened the door for women to be appointed to the Senate, and it continues to inspire efforts toward equality and representation in Canada today.
PETAL: It's tulip time in Ottawa! Every May, over a million tulip petals pop open across the capital for the [Canadian Tulip Festival](https://tulipfestival.ca/) - a blooming beautiful tradition that started with a royal thank-you. Back in 1945, the Dutch royal family sent 100,000 tulip bulbs to Canada to show their gratitude for sheltering Princess Juliana and her daughters during World War II. To ensure Princess Margriet was born a Dutch citizen, the maternity ward at the Ottawa Civic Hospital was temporarily declared international territory. That act of kindness planted the seeds of a friendship that still blossoms today - one tulip petal at a time!
PETTY: Petty Harbour-Maddox Cove is a picturesque fishing village located on the eastern shore of Newfoundland and Labrador, just south of St. John's. This charming community is known for its colourful row houses, stunning coastal views, and rich maritime history. Petty Harbour is not only a haven for fishermen but also a popular spot for tourists seeking to experience Newfoundland's natural beauty and vibrant culture. The village has been featured in various films and television shows, showcasing its stunning landscapes and traditional fishing practices.
PHLOX: Tall, vibrantly coloured summer-flowering phlox is one of the most popular garden perennials in Canada. Phlox is often used for island beds or as border plants. Many flower colours are available and most produce a sweet fragrance during the July-September flowering period. Phlox is a wide-ranging North American native perennial and a common fixture in woodland, prairie, and meadow landscapes.
PHOCA: Canada’s coasts and Arctic waters are home to phoca, the earless seals that delight with their curious eyes and playful antics. From harbour seals lounging on rocky shores to spotted seals gliding through northern ice, these whiskered swimmers are a lively and unforgettable part of Canada’s marine wildlife.
PIANO: Canada has a storied piano making past, and was home to more than 100 piano manufacturing companies during the peak era of the industry. Piano building in Canada began in the early 19th century and grew into a major, thriving industry between 1890 and 1925. Many Canadians have become noted pianists. Glenn Gould is a bona fide Canadian icon who became one of the most famous and celebrated classical pianists of the 20th century, while Oscar Peterson has had an equally influential role in jazz piano and is considered one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. Other notable Canadian pianists include Angela Hewitt, Chantal Kreviazuk, Diana Krall, Marc-André Hamelin, Anton Kuerti, Charles Richard-Hamelin, and Jan Lisiecki.
PILOT: One of Canada's most famous pilots, Billy Bishop was a Canadian flying ace of the First World War. He was officially credited with 72 victories, making him the top Canadian and British Empire ace of the war. The Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport was named in his honour. Today would have been Billy Bishop's 129th birthday!
PINCH: Happy St. Patrick's Day from O'Canuckle! According to fun folklore, you get pinched on St. Patrick's Day for not wearing green because green makes you invisible to leprechauns. Leprechauns are mischievous creatures, and according to legend, they like to pinch people. Canada's first St. Patrick's Day parade was held in Montreal in 1824. Ever since, parades and festivals of Irish culture have been held annually on March 17th in cities across Canada.
PINES: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! The Scotch pine reigns as the top Christmas tree in Canada. Scotch pines hardly shed any of their long needles, and their strong, curved branches also hold ornaments well. Canada exported over 2.4 million fresh Christmas trees to countries all over the world in 2021! Pines are the also the arboreal emblem of the provinces of Alberta (Lodgepole pine) and Ontario (Eastern white pine).
PINOT: Pinot grapes have found a home in Canada’s wine regions, including British Columbia’s Okanagan Valley and Ontario’s Niagara Peninsula. Varieties like Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris have helped Canadian winemakers showcase the country’s unique climates and growing conditions.
PIPES: Canada has a long tradition of bagpipe music, especially in communities with strong Scottish roots. Pipe bands are a familiar sight at parades, ceremonies, and Highland games across the country. The [Glengarry Highland Games](https://www.glengarryhighlandgames.com/) in Maxville, Ontario, are one of the largest gatherings of their kind in North America, hosting competitions in piping, drumming, Highland dancing, and heavy athletics. From coast to coast, Canadian pipers help keep this centuries-old musical tradition alive and thriving.
PIPIT: The [Sprague’s Pipit](https://naturecounts.ca/nc/socb-epoc/species.jsp?sp=sprpip) is a small prairie bird with a remarkable song, delivering a long, silvery cascade of notes while soaring high above the grasslands. Canada is home to roughly 80% of the world’s breeding population, found mainly in the native prairies of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Once widespread, the species has declined sharply and is now listed as Threatened under Canada’s Species at Risk Act.
PISTE: In modern [fencing](https://www.fencing.ca), the "piste" is the narrow strip on which fencers duel, and Canadian athletes have shown remarkable prowess on it! At the 2024 Paris Olympics, [Eleanor Harvey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/eleanor-harvey/) made history by winning a bronze medal in women’s individual foil, marking the first fencing medal ever for Canada in this elegant sport!
PLANE: Aviation is an integral part of the Canadian economy. In 2018, the air transport industry, including airlines, and its supply chain, supported over $50 billion of GDP in Canada.
PLANT: The [Bruce Nuclear Generating Station](https://www.brucepower.com/) is a nuclear power plant located on the eastern shore of Lake Huron in Ontario. With eight CANDU pressurized heavy-water reactors, it is the largest operating nuclear power plant in the world! The plant is the largest employer in Bruce County, with over 4000 workers.
PLUNGE: Canadians are famous for plunging into the New Year with polar plunges held in icy waters across the country. From lakes to oceans, these frosty traditions combine community spirit, charitable causes, and a fearless embrace of winter – a very Canadian way to kick off January.
PODGE: Hodge podge is a favourite vegetable stew from Nova Scotia. Hodge podge originally comes from Acadians living in Nova Scotia who would harvest their vegetables at the height of summer from their garden and immediately make them into a soup using butter and cream. Hodge podge is basic, soul warming food, that celebrates fresh produce - it's a true East Coast classic!
PODIA: At the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milano‑Cortina, Canadian athletes stood proudly on multiple podia (the platforms where medalists celebrate their achievements) – each one a story of grit and grace. Those medal moments reminded fans that Canada’s colours shine brightest when the world’s best gather for the Games. Every podium captured the excitement, skill, and national pride of Canadians on the world’s biggest winter stage. Congratulations to all of the Team Canada athletes!
POETS: Canadian poets have made significant contributions to the world of literature, weaving tales of diverse landscapes, cultures, and identities. From renowned figures like Margaret Atwood and Leonard Cohen to emerging talents, Canadian poets captivate readers with their lyrical prowess and thought-provoking verses, celebrating the nation’s rich poetic tapestry. Visit [poets.ca](https://poets.ca/) to learn more about the League of Canadian Poets supporting poets and poetry in Canada!
POINT: Point Pelee is the southernmost point of mainland Canada, and is an important rest stop for migrating birds. [Point Pelee National Park](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/on/pelee) is Canada's second smallest but most ecologically diverse national park, and is home to more than 390 bird species and 70 species of trees, some of which are species at risk.
POLAR: Canada is home to about 16,000 polar bears, which is approximately two-thirds of the world's total estimated population.
PORTS: Canada is home to numerous ports, but the Port of Vancouver is Canada's largest port, and is the most diversified port in North America.
POSTS: Founded in 1670, the Hudson’s Bay Company built hundreds of [trading posts](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/hbc-trading-posts-in-canada) across what is now Canada, often along rivers and lakes that served as important transportation routes. These remote outposts became centres of trade and communication, exchanging European goods for furs with Indigenous peoples and helping shape the growth of communities across the country.
POUCH: [Pouch Cove](https://pouchcove.ca/), Newfoundland & Labrador, is a friendly town on the northern tip of the Avalon Peninsula, neighbouring Torbay, Flatrock, and Bauline. Known as the place “first to see the sun” in North America, it’s also a gateway to the East Coast Trail, with rugged hikes like the Biscan Cove and Stiles Cove paths offering breathtaking ocean views.
POUND: Lobster season has officially started in Canada in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Canada currently supplies more than half of the world’s supply of “hard-shelled” Atlantic Lobster, considered one of the world’s premier seafood. A lobster pound is where live lobsters are held until they are harvested and sold, like at [Halls Harbour Lobster Pound](https://hallsharbourlobster.com/) in Nova Scotia and [Lobster on the Wharf](https://www.lobsteronthewharf.com/) in PEI, known as MacKinnon's Lobster Pound to locals.
PRANK: April Fools' Day wouldn't be the same without a classic prank, and one of the most iconic prank devices, the whoopee cushion, was invented in Toronto in the 1930s! Created by the JEM Rubber Company, this cheeky contraption has been a prankster's favourite for nearly 100 years, delivering laughs and a few embarrassed giggles along the way. A simple but brilliant invention, the whoopee cushion proves that a well-placed prank never goes out of style!
PRINT: Happy Labour Day! Labour Day has been marked as a statutory public holiday in Canada on the first Monday in September since 1894. However, the origins of Labour Day in Canada can be traced back to numerous local demonstrations and celebrations in earlier decades. Such events assumed political significance in 1872, when an April labour demonstration in Toronto, in support of the printers of the Toronto Typographical Union on strike for a nine-hour day, led directly to the enactment of the Trade Unions Act, a law that confirmed the legality of unions. The Printers' Strike of 1872, part of the Nine Hour Movement, was a key moment in Canadian labour history and marked the start of a shorter workday.
PRIVY: The [Privy Council Office](https://www.canada.ca/en/privy-council.html) is the central agency of the Government of Canada which acts as the secretariat to the Cabinet of Canada and provides non-partisan advice and support to the Canadian ministry. The clerk of the Privy Council, who leads the department, is the head of the civil service of Canada, and acts as Deputy Minister to the Prime Minister.
PRONG: Built for speed, pronghorns are the fastest land mammals in Canada, capable of reaching speeds of up to 90 km/h across the open prairies of southern Alberta and Saskatchewan. Their signature “prongs” are especially rare in the animal kingdom – true horns that shed and regrow each year, unlike the permanent horns of most animals.
PULSE: Pulses are nitrogen-fixing crops that improve the environmental sustainability of cropping systems. Canada is one of the largest pulse producers in the world and the largest exporter, with over 80% of pulses grown being shipped around the world. The four main types of pulses grown in Canada are dry peas, lentils, chickpeas and beans. Learn more at [pulsecanada.com](https://pulsecanada.com/)!
PUREE: Pumpkin pie is a beloved dessert for Thanksgiving in Canada, and it often features pumpkin puree as a key ingredient. This smooth, sweet mixture is essential for making delicious pumpkin pie, a favourite dessert on Canadian Thanksgiving tables. In fact, 60% of Canadians indulge in this delightful dessert every Thanksgiving, highlighting its popularity across the country. Whether you're using fresh pumpkins or canned puree, this comforting dessert is sure to bring warmth and joy to Thanksgiving celebrations.
PURSE: Long before modern handbags, Indigenous artisans across Canada crafted beautiful and functional purses using materials from the land. Caribou hide was carefully prepared for durability and softness, then adorned with intricate glass beadwork introduced through early trade. These handmade purses were not only practical – they often carried deep cultural meaning, with patterns and colours reflecting identity, community, and tradition.
QUAKE: Seismologists locate more than 4000 earthquakes every year in Canada and the surrounding areas. Thankfully most of these earthquakes are smaller than magnitude 3 and are not felt. Government of Canada monitoring and research on earthquakes is undertaken by Natural Resources Canada’s Earth Sciences Sector. For more information on earthquakes visit the Geological Survey of Canada, NRCan website: earthquakescanada.ca
QUESO: Queso might be a Tex-Mex favourite, but one of Canada’s go-to spots is homegrown! [Lone Star Texas Grill](https://lonestartexasgrill.com/) opened its first Ottawa location in 1986, serving up warm queso dip, fresh tortilla chips, and sizzling fajitas. Nearly 40 years later, it’s still proudly Canadian-owned – with a Texas twist that’s earned fans from coast to coast.
QUILT: Quilts were extremely important to the early settlers of Canada, since they had no good way of heating or insulating their homes, especially at night. The first quilts arrived in Canada with immigrants to "New France" in the early 1600s. Today, the [Canadian Quilters' Association](https://canadianquilter.com/) celebrates quilting and Canadian quilters across the country.
RADAR: Perched in the heart of Huron at the junction of Highways 4 and 8 is the iconic radar antenna that has forever identified Clinton, Ontario as '[the Home of Radar](https://www.stopsalongtheway.ca/clinton-monument)' in Canada. The antenna is part of the AN/FPS-20 long range radar system and is a relic of the Cold War. It was originally donated by the Canadian Forces Base Clinton in 1967 in honour of the Canadian Centennial as a monument to the country and the people trained at the base. The base was Canada's first radar school, opening in August 1941, and the site trained nearly 9,000 students by the end of World War II: more than 6,500 Canadians and over 2,300 Americans.
RADII: Radii are the lines from the centre to the edge of a circle – the building blocks of Pi, celebrated worldwide on March 14. In Canada, math lovers mark Pi Day with everything from circular pancakes to STEM activities, and Canadian mathematician John Charles Fields, namesake of the prestigious Fields Medal, reminds us that understanding radii is key to the discoveries honoured at the highest levels of mathematics.
RAISE: Yesterday would have been Terry Fox's 65th birthday! Terry Fox is one of the most prominent figures in all of Canada. In 1977, 18-year-old Terry Fox was diagnosed with bone cancer and gave up his right leg to prevent the spread of the disease. The Canadian Cancer Society helped sponsor his run across Canada to raise funds and awareness for cancer research. The Marathon of Hope raised $24.2 million for cancer research and Terry became an inspiration to millions of people worldwide. To date, the [Terry Fox Foundation](https://terryfox.org/) has raised over 600 million dollars for cancer research.
RANCH: Cattle ranching is the most common type of ranching in Canada, with over 70% of ranches raising beef cattle. Canada is the fourth-largest beef and cattle exporter in the world, with over 60,000 cattle farms and ranches. There are approximately 3.7 million beef cattle in Canada, of which nearly half are in Alberta.
RAPID: The [Reversing Falls](https://tourismnewbrunswick.ca/listing/reversing-falls-rapids) are a series of rapids on the Saint John River located in Saint John, New Brunswick, where the river runs through a narrow gorge before emptying into the Bay of Fundy. The amazing phenomenon of the Reversing Falls Rapids is a sight to behold. If you time it just right, you can watch the Bay of Fundy’s monstrously high tide reverse the flow of the mighty Saint John River.
REBAR: Rebar (short for "reinforcing bar") is a key material in construction, providing strength and durability to concrete structures. Canada has a strong steel industry, with major production hubs in Ontario, Quebec, and Alberta supplying high-quality rebar for bridges, buildings, and infrastructure projects across the country. Many Canadian steel mills, such as those in Hamilton, Ontario (nicknamed "Steeltown") manufacture rebar using recycled steel, making it both strong and sustainable! So whether it's a towering skyscraper or a sturdy hockey arena, Canadian-made rebar helps build the backbone of our nation!
RELIC: Robert Allan Clothier was a Canadian stage and television actor most famous for his role as Relic on the CBC television series, The Beachcombers. He portrayed Bruno Gerussi's rival beachcomber, Relic - a curmudgeonly, conniving man of Welsh descent who lived on a house boat and used his jetboat to outrun and challenge Nick's claims to logs. After landing this memorable role, Clothier became a household face among viewers, as the show originally aired from 1972 to 1990, one of the longest running Canadian television dramas of all time.
RIDER: [Canadian equestrian](https://equestrian.ca/) riders have shone brightly on the world stage in both dressage and eventing! [Ian Millar](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/ian-millar/), affectionately known as "Captain Canada," has competed in a record 10 Olympic Games, winning a team silver medal in show jumping at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. In dressage, Canada brought home a bronze medal in team dressage from the 1988 Seoul Olympics. Canada’s equestrian success continues to inspire and showcase the dedication and talent of its riders.
RIFLE: [The Queen's Own Rifles of Canada](https://www.queensownrifles.com/) is a Primary Army Reserve infantry regiment based in Toronto. Founded on April 26th, 1860, it is the oldest continuously serving infantry regiment in Canada. Its members have served in every Canadian military campaign and served with great distinction in World War I and World War II in which 7 Riflemen were awarded the Victoria Cross.
RIGHT: The [Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/csj-sjc/rfc-dlc/ccrf-ccdl/) protects a number of rights and freedoms, including freedom of expression and the right to equality. It forms part of our Constitution – the highest law in all of Canada – and is one of our country’s greatest accomplishments. Every year on April 17th, we celebrate the anniversary of the Charter which was signed in 1982.
ROARS: Every September, the tiny community of Elliston, Newfoundland and Labrador, comes alive for [Roots, Rants and Roars](https://www.rootsrantsandroars.ca/). Known as the Root Cellar Capital of the World, Elliston hosts this celebration of the province’s food, culture, land and sea. Hundreds of guests hike a rugged 5 km coastal trail, stopping along the way to sample dishes prepared by top chefs using locally harvested and foraged ingredients. The festival also features Cod Wars, a lively culinary showdown celebrating the fish that has shaped the province for generations.
ROBOT: Canada has a thriving robotics industry, and many of the most famous and inventive real-world robots have Canadian origins, many of which have taken to the stars. The iconic Canadarm & Canadarm 2 robotic arms have supported space shuttle missions for decades, and Dextre is a versatile robot that maintains the International Space Station (ISS). Part of Canada's contribution to the Station, it is the most sophisticated space robot ever built.
ROUGE: In the Canadian Football League (CFL), a rouge is a one-point score that is awarded for certain plays that involve the ball being kicked into the end zone. The rouge is uniquely Canadian!
ROUGH: The Canadian Football League (CFL) once had two teams with nearly identical names: the Ottawa Rough Riders and the Saskatchewan Roughriders. This led to some confusion among fans and broadcasters, especially during games between the two teams. In 1996, the Ottawa team folded, leaving Saskatchewan as the sole "Roughriders" in the CFL. The Ottawa franchise returned in 2002 as the Ottawa Renegades, and later became the Ottawa Redblacks in 2014. Despite the name changes, the legacy of the "Rough Riders" and "Roughriders" remains a unique chapter in Canadian football history.
ROUSE: "The Rouse" is a bugle call most often associated with the military in Commonwealth countries. It is commonly played following "Last Post" at military services. "The Rouse" was traditionally played following "Reveille", which was a bugle call played in the morning to wake soldiers up.
ROVER: Canada is gearing up to send its very first lunar rover to the Moon! As part of NASA’s Artemis program, the [Canadian Lunar Rover](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronomy/moon-exploration/first-canadian-rover-to-explore-the-moon.asp) will explore the Moon’s surface, conducting experiments and collecting valuable data. This innovative rover, developed by the Canadian Space Agency, highlights Canada's continued leadership in space exploration. The rover will carry forward Canada's proud legacy, from the Apollo missions’ Lunar Roving Vehicle to this next chapter in lunar discovery.
RUDDY: The Ruddy Duck is one of Canada’s smallest diving ducks, with a compact chestnut body, sky-blue bill, and stiff, upright tail. About 86% of its breeding population nests in wetlands and reservoirs of the prairie pothole region. Males are known for lively courtship displays, sometimes drumming the water with their bills to impress a mate!
RUGBY: Buoyed by its inclusion in the 2016 Olympic Games, Rugby is one of the fastest growing team sports in Canada, particularly in youth and women.
SABRE: The Canadian-built [Canadair Sabre](https://ingeniumcanada.org/aviation/artifact/canadair-sabre-6) was a single-engine jet fighter flown by the Golden Hawks - the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aerobatic flying team that preceded the Snowbirds. The Sabre was able to reach supersonic speeds in dives - first achieved in Canada by test pilot Al Lilly in 1950 when he broke the sound barrier flying a Canadair Sabre prototype. The Sabre had a distinctive gold livery with a red and white hawk painted on each side of the fuselage that captivated airshow crowds across Canada.
SANTA: HO HO HO! Did you know that Santa Claus is a legal Canadian citizen? Santa was declared a full Canadian citizen in 2008 by Canada’s Immigration Minister and was even issued a Canadian passport in 2013! Of course, Santa also has the most famous postal code in Canada: H0H 0H0. Santa's closest neighbours are the Canadians living in Alert, Nunavut, only 820 kilometres from the North Pole. Merry Christmas, eh?
SCOFF: Scoff is Newfoundland slang for a big feed, typically Jiggs dinner but could be any large, satisfying meal.
SCOPE: It's [Canadian Innovation Week](https://canadianinnovationspace.ca/)! Did you know that Canada played a significant role in the development of the James Webb Space Telescope? The [Canadian Space Agency](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/) contributed two important elements, built by Honeywell: the Fine Guidance Sensor (FGS), which allows the telescope to point at and focus on objects of interest, and the Near-Infrared Imager and Slitless Spectrograph (NIRISS), a scientific instrument that helps study many astronomical objects, from exoplanets to distant galaxies. Canada receives a guaranteed share of Webb's observation time, making Canadian scientists some of the first to study data collected by the most advanced space telescope ever built.
SEALS: Seals are found in the waters of all three Canadian oceans: harbour in both Pacific and Atlantic; bearded and ringed in the Arctic; harp and hooded in the North Atlantic and parts of the Arctic; and grey in Atlantic Canada.
SEATS: Today is [Election Day](https://www.elections.ca/)! In Canada's 2025 federal election, the House of Commons expanded to 343 seats, reflecting the country's growing population. This change underscores the dynamic nature of Canada's democracy, ensuring that representation in Parliament keeps pace with demographic shifts. Each seat represents a unique riding, and the party that secures at least 172 seats forms a majority government. This adjustment emphasizes the importance of every vote, as even a single seat can influence the balance of power in Parliament.
SEDGE: In Canada, marshy areas known as sedges are important habitats for wildlife, especially for cranes! The term "sedge" not only refers to grassy wetlands but also to a group of cranes gathering in these lush areas. Canada is home to two species of cranes - the Sandhill Crane and the endangered Whooping Crane. Each fall, Sandhill Cranes flock to Canadian wetlands, where sedges provide the perfect mix of cover and food as they prepare for migration. These crane gatherings are a beautiful sight, showcasing how Canada’s diverse ecosystems support unique wildlife year-round.
SEINE: Seine net fishing has been one of the most important methods used on Canada’s Pacific and Atlantic coasts for generations. A seine net encircles a school of fish such as salmon, herring, or mackerel, then closes like a drawstring purse at the bottom. Commonly used by purse seiners in British Columbia during salmon season, the technique has deep roots in both Indigenous and settler fishing traditions and remains a key part of Canada’s coastal fisheries today.
SEPAL: Sepal is the part of a flower that protects a developing bloom before it opens, forming the green base that supports the petals inside. In Ottawa, over one million tulips begin to emerge as the [Canadian Tulip Festival](https://tulipfestival.ca/) gets underway, marking the start of one of Canada’s most colourful spring celebrations. Each tulip relies on its sepal in those early stages to protect the bud before it unfurls into full bloom for festival visitors to enjoy.
SEWED: On [National Flag of Canada Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/national-flag-canada-day.html), we remember the woman who literally sewed Canada’s identity into history. In 1964, Ottawa civil servant Joan O’Malley stayed late into the night at her Singer sewing machine to sew the first Canadian flag, turning cloth and thread into a symbol that would unite a nation. Every stitch carried pride, purpose, and the promise of a flag that would fly over homes, schools, and Parliament – and, of course, soar above Canadian athletes at the Olympics!
SHACK: The end of March means it's time to visit a sugar shack in Canada! Sugar shacks ("cabanes à sucres" in French) are cabins where sap is collected from sugar maple trees and boiled into maple syrup through a technique originally developed by the Indigenous and passed on to the French colonizers of New-France. If you are visiting Canada, don't miss your chance to experience an authentic sugar shack meal, where everything is drowned in maple syrup!
SHAKO: The shako is a tall, cylindrical military cap once commonly worn by rifle regiments, including the [Queen’s Own Rifles of Canada](https://www.queensownrifles.com/). In the 19th century, it was part of the formal uniform for officers and soldiers alike. The shako often features a cap badge displaying a crowned bugle horn – a symbol of light infantry and rifle regiments – along with the regiment’s name, reflecting a proud tradition of bravery and service.
SHEER: Percé Rock is a huge sheer rock formation in the Gulf of Saint Lawrence on the tip of the Gaspé Peninsula in Quebec. Percé Rock appears from a distance like a ship under sail. It is one of the world's largest natural arches located in water and is considered a geologically and historically rich natural icon of Quebec.
SHERO: Today is International Women's Day! It's a day to celebrate the incredible women who inspire us with their strength, courage, and resilience. The term "shero" blends "she" and "hero," recognizing the powerful impact women have had across the world. From groundbreaking scientists like Canada's Dr. Roberta Bondar, the first Canadian woman in space, to civil rights pioneers like Viola Desmond, who fought for racial equality in Nova Scotia, women continue to shape history and break barriers. Let's honour these amazing women today and every day, as they empower future generations with their courage and determination!
SIEGE: The Siege of Québec was a pivotal three-month military campaign during the Seven Years’ War that helped lay the foundation for modern Canada. From June 26 to September 18, 1759, British forces besieged the city before defeating French forces in the [Battle of the Plains of Abraham](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/battle-of-the-plains-of-abraham). The victory led to British control of New France and a realignment of alliances with First Nations.
SILLY: Being silly is a proud Canadian tradition. Canadians invented the modern Whoopee Cushion in Toronto in the 1930s, and since then, April Fools’ Day has been celebrated with funny news stories, cheeky tricks, and harmless pranks across the country. From silly shenanigans to playful jokes among friends, Canada’s tradition of silliness keeps the laughs rolling every April 1.
SILVER: Canada’s silver rush began near [Cobalt, Ontario](https://cobalt.ca/), in 1903, sparking a mining boom that transformed the small northern community into one of the world’s great silver-producing regions. Cobalt’s mines yielded millions of ounces of silver each year, earning the town the nickname “Silver Capital of Canada.” The rush attracted thousands of prospectors and miners, and the wealth and expertise generated there helped fuel the development of mining across northern Ontario.
SKARN: A skarn is a type of metamorphic rock that forms when hot magma interacts with surrounding limestone or dolostone. This contact creates new minerals, often rich in metals like copper, gold, and tungsten. In Canada, skarn deposits have been significant in mining areas like British Columbia and Quebec, where valuable ores are extracted. Skarns highlight how geological processes transform rocks into mineral-rich resources that play an important role in the mining industry!
SKATE: Skate Canada is the oldest and largest figure skating organization in the world.
SKEIN: A skein is a group of geese flying together in a "V" shaped formation. In the sky, they are called skein, but when a flock of geese is on the ground, they form a gaggle. Did you know that a skein of migrating Canada geese can fly up to 2,400 km in 24 hours? Canada geese travel north between April and early June, so look up in the sky to spot a skein and listen for their distinctive honks!
SKIES: The Prairie Skies were voted one of [Canada's Seven Wonders](https://www.cbc.ca/sevenwonders/) in a 2007 competition sponsored by CBC Television's The National and CBC Radio One's Sounds Like Canada. Rounding out the list of Canada's Seven Wonders were Niagara Falls, Halifax's Pier 21, The Rockies, Old Quebec, the igloo, and the canoe. The province of Saskatchewan is known as the "Land of Living Skies" and even features the slogan on its provincial license plates.
SKINK: The Common Five-lined Skink is one of Canada's native lizard species. Found in Ontario along the southern edge of the Canadian Shield, these small, speedy reptiles prefer warm, rocky habitats and forested areas. Juveniles are especially eye-catching with their bright blue tails, which they can detach to escape predators - a clever survival trick! While their tails eventually regrow, it takes a lot of energy, so they don't drop them unless absolutely necessary. As a cold-blooded species, skinks bask in the sun to stay warm, making them a rare but fascinating sight in the Canadian wild!
SKIPS: In the sport of curling, the skip is the captain of a team. The skip determines strategy, and holds the broom in the house to indicate where a teammate at the other end of the curling sheet should aim the stone. Canada is home to some of the best curling skips in the world, including household names like Jennifer Jones, Kevin Martin, Sandra Schmirler, Russ & Glenn Howard, Colleen Jones, Ernie Richardson, Randy Ferbey, Connie Laliberte, Jeff Stoughton, Rachel Homan, Kevin Koe, Kerri Einarson and Brad Gushue.
SLACK: [Slack](https://slack.com/), the popular cloud-based collaboration tool used by millions worldwide, was co-created by Canadian entrepreneur Stewart Butterfield! Originally from Lund, British Columbia, Butterfield launched Slack in 2013, revolutionizing how teams communicate and work together online. The product name Slack was derived from the phrase "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Today, Slack is an essential tool for businesses and organizations, enabling seamless messaging, file sharing, and project management.
SLATE: In Canada’s early one-room schoolhouses, students didn’t have notebooks or tablets – they used slates! These small, handheld chalkboards were a reusable and affordable way for kids to practise writing and arithmetic. With a slate pencil in hand, students could solve math problems, copy sentences, or spell out their lessons, then simply wipe it clean and start again. Slates were especially common in rural schools, where supplies were scarce and learning had to be practical. It’s a little piece of classroom history that helped shape generations of Canadian students!
SLEDS: “Toboggan” is from the Mi'kmaq word “tobakun,” which means sled. In fact, the Inuit made the first toboggans out of whale bone and used it to transport people and belongings across the snowy tundra. Guy Martin holds the world record for fastest speed on a gravity powered snow sled at over 134 km/h in 2014!
SMILE: Canadians have lots of reasons to smile! Canada is the 13th happiest country in the world out of 157 countries ranked according to the 2023 World Happiness Report. This week is [Smile Cookie](https://www.timhortons.ca/smile-cookie) week at Tim Hortons! From May 1st through May 7th, 100% of proceeds from every Smile Cookie support charities and community groups across Canada. The Smile Cookie campaign has raised over $92 million across North America since 1996 and last year, restaurant owners raised a record-breaking $15 million! Get your #SmileCookie this week and put a smile on someone's face!
SMOKE: Today is National Indigenous Peoples Day! Smoke is used in different ways by all three Indigenous groups in Canada. Whether it is to smoke fish and meat, to burn sage and tobacco or for sacred ceremonies or celebrations, it is a significant symbol in Indigenous culture.
SNACK: June 7 is National Donut Day! Donuts are one of Canada's most beloved snack foods and these sweet treats have become a staple of Canadian culture. In fact, Canada has the most donut shops and consumes the most donuts per capita of any other country in the world - around 1 billion annually! Whether you prefer a classic style donut or a more elaborate creation, donuts hold a special place in the hearts (and stomachs) of Canadians from coast to coast.
SNOWY: On February 10, 1999, Tahtsa Lake, British Columbia got hit with 145 cm (4'9") of snow in ONE day!
SOBER: Each January, many Canadians take part in Dry January, giving up alcohol for the month to reset after the holidays and start the year feeling clearer and healthier. Around 41% of Canadian adults either participate or cut back during January, showing just how popular the sober start has become. One flavour-forward option is [Sober Carpenter](https://sobercarpenter.com/), a Canadian non-alcoholic craft beer founded in Québec, brewing alcohol-free beers that let Canadians stay social while staying sober.
SOLVE: Yesterday was National Puzzle Day! Each year on January 29th, National Puzzle Day recognizes how exercising our brains with puzzles is just one of its many benefits. It's the perfect day to solve some puzzles and do a little brain exercise! Whether it’s a solving a jigsaw, a word game like [Canuckle](https://www.canucklegame.ca) or a sudoku game like Canoku, puzzles engage our brain in more ways than one. We've even launched a new Brain Health Edition of Canoku - check it out at brainhealth.canoku.ca and give your brain a boost! 🧠💪
SONNY: “Sonny’s Dream” is a beloved Canadian folk song written by Newfoundland singer-songwriter Ron Hynes. Released in 1976, the song tells the story of a young person dreaming of a better life while staying connected to home. It gained international recognition through recordings by artists such as Mary Black and The Rankin Family.
SOUTH: The Great White...South? Point Pelee is the southernmost point of mainland Canada, and is located on a foundation of glacial sand, silt and gravel that bites into Lake Erie. The word pelée is French for 'bald'. Point Pelee was the first national park in Canada to be established for conservation. The national park lies on the 42nd Parallel, making it the same latitude as northern California, Barcelona and Rome.
SPAWN: Every fall, Canada's rivers and streams come alive with the incredible sight of salmon spawning! These resilient fish travel upstream, often covering hundreds of kilometres, to lay their eggs in the same waters where they were born. British Columbia's Fraser River is one of the most famous spawning grounds in the world, where millions of sockeye salmon return each year. This natural cycle is crucial to the ecosystem, supporting wildlife from eagles to bears. Watching the salmon spawn is a quintessential Canadian experience and a celebration of nature's perseverance!
SPICE: Emerging spice crops in Saskatchewan include coriander, caraway, dill, anise, and fenugreek, but mustard seed is the most important spice crop in Saskatchewan. Canada is the second largest producer in the world with over 200,000 tonnes per year, and the largest exporter with 160,000 tonnes per year. Saskatchewan produces 80–90% of the Canadian mustard seed and is known worldwide for the production of a high-quality product.
SPILE: A spile is a tube mechanism that you tap into a tree to collect sap, which in turn can be evaporated and boiled for delicious maple syrup!
SPINY: Canada's most unique terrestrial animal is probably not what you might think. A recent study published in the journal The [Canadian Field-Naturalist](https://www.canadianfieldnaturalist.ca/index.php/cfn/article/view/2673) has found the country's most evolutionarily distinct Canadian animal is the spiny softshell turtle! These turtles can be found in Ontario and Quebec, and are one of the largest freshwater turtle species in North America. But unfortunately, they have been listed as one of Canada's rarest species for over 20 years. If we let them disappear from Canada, we would lose almost 180 million years of unique evolutionary history. This shows how important it is to prioritize the conservation of this species and its unique legacy amongst Canadian wildlife.
SPOOR: In Canada, spoor refers to the tracks or signs left by animals in the wild, like deer, moose, wolves, or lynx. From snow-covered forests to muddy riverbanks, following spoor has helped naturalists, trappers, and Indigenous communities study and track wildlife for generations. In the Canadian wilderness, where vast forests and frozen landscapes can make spotting wildlife difficult, spoor provides a hidden map of animal life waiting to be discovered.
SPORT: Canada's official national sports are ice hockey (winter) and lacrosse (summer).
STACK: The Hopewell Rocks in New Brunswick (also known as flowerpots) are rock formations known as sea stacks caused by tidal erosion. They are located on the shores of the Bay of Fundy in [Hopewell Rocks Provincial Park](https://www.nbparks.ca/en/parks/33/hopewell-rocks-provincial-park) and come in an astounding variety of shapes and sizes. No Atlantic Canadian vacation is complete without experiencing these icons!
STALL: The [Richmond Night Market](https://www.richmondnightmarket.com/) in Richmond, BC, is the largest night market in North America, inspired by the vibrant night markets of Asia. Open seasonally from spring to fall, it packs more than 200 food and retail stalls into a bustling outdoor venue and attracts over one million visitors each year. From sizzling street food and sweet treats to games and unique finds, there’s something new waiting at almost every stall.
STAMP: The Three-Pence Beaver was Canada's first postage stamp in 1851. It was the first stamp in the world to feature an animal. The beaver building a dam was symbolic of the people in the young country of Canada building their towns, cities, and communities.
START: In 2025, [Canadian Tire’s Jumpstart program](https://jumpstart.canadiantire.ca/) celebrates 20 years of helping kids across Canada start their journey in sports by removing financial barriers. Since 2005, Jumpstart has provided funding for equipment, registration fees, and transportation so thousands of children can get active, build confidence, and feel part of their communities. Getting a great start in sports helps kids grow stronger – on the field and off.
STAVE: The NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs began on Saturday, April 18, launching a grueling postseason where every series is a best-of-seven battle. From coast to coast to coast, teams will try to stave off elimination in pursuit of the Stanley Cup, arguably the hardest trophy in sports to win. Canadian fans will be cheering on their teams throughout the chase for hockey’s ultimate prize.
STEAM: Steam transportation allowed people in Canada to move beyond their immediate communities and interact with a wider world. The years from 1900 to 1960 were the last great age of steam locomotion. Steamships and steam-powered railways were at the height of their power, efficiency, and reliability. These technologies were fundamental to the lives of Canadians.
STEER: At the [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/), steer wrestling is a fan-favourite event that puts cowboy courage to the test! In this thrilling rodeo challenge, a rider leaps from a galloping horse and attempts to wrestle a sprinting steer to the ground using strength, speed, and precision. It’s a heart-pounding highlight of the Stampede, showcasing the daring skills rooted in Canada’s ranching traditions.
STERN: Located in Kaslo, British Columbia, the [S.S. Moyie stern wheeler](https://www.klhs.bc.ca/) is the oldest intact passenger steam vessel of its type in the world. The machinery and the steel frames of its hull were built by the Bertram Engine Works of Toronto, shipped west by rail and assembled in Vancouver. Launched at Nelson on 22 October 1898 by the Canadian Pacific Railway, the S.S. Moyie carried passengers and freight on Kootenay Lake for 59 years. It was retired from service in 1957. Rescued and preserved by the people of Kaslo, the "sweetheart of the lake" recalls the role of sternwheelers in the history of western Canada. 2023 marks the 125th birthday celebration of the S.S. Moyie, which was designated a national historic site of Canada in 1958 and reaffirmed in 1983.
STICK: Hockey and Canada are synonymous with each other, and the sport remains integral to the country’s culture. Hockey sticks go back to the 1800’s where sticks were hand carved from a single piece of wood. The first commercial sticks were said to be created by the Mi’kmaq carvers in Nova Scotia and were made from birch and hornbeam trees.
STILL: [Still: A Michael J. Fox Movie](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt19853258/) is a 2023 documentary about a short kid from a Canadian army base that becomes the international pop culture darling of the 1980s - only to find the course of his life altered by a stunning diagnosis. Winner of 4 Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Documentary, Still follows the life of beloved actor and advocate Michael J. Fox, exploring his personal and professional triumphs and travails, and what happens when an incurable optimist confronts an incurable disease.
STING: Today marks the start of the [Ontario Hockey League](https://chl.ca/ohl/) (OHL) regular season in Canada! The [Sarnia Sting](https://chl.ca/ohl-sting/) are a junior ice hockey team based in Sarnia, Ontario. They are one of the 20 teams that make up the OHL. The franchise was granted in 1969 as one of the inaugural teams of the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League. At the time, the team was located in Cornwall, Ontario and known as the Cornwall Royals.
STOCK: The Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) is a stock exchange located in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. It is the 10th largest exchange in the world and the third largest in North America based on market capitalization. The Montreal Exchange is Canada's oldest exchange and was formerly called the Montreal Stock Exchange.
STONE: A building material used in Manitoba for nearly 200 years, from trading forts to the modern-day architecture of the Canadian Museum for Human Rights, received international recognition in 2023 as a global heritage stone resource.
