Tyndall Stone - a fossil-laden limestone dating back 450 million years - has also been used at the parliament buildings in Ottawa, the Canadian Museum of History in Quebec and the legislative buildings in Regina and Winnipeg. Canada is the only source in the world for the stone, and Manitoba is the only place it is quarried. The designation means that the Tyndall stone is considered a culturally significant material.
STONY: [Stony Plain](https://www.stonyplain.com/) is a town in the Edmonton Metropolitan Region of Alberta that is situated on the traditional lands of Treaty 6 peoples. Stony Plain is known for its many painted murals representing various periods, events and people throughout the town's history. The town was originally known as Dog Rump Creek. Stony Plain is also home to [Canadian History Ehx](https://canadaehx.com/) podcaster and historian, [Craig Baird](https://x.com/CraigBaird), who explores the good, the bad and the weird of Canada's history. Join Canuckle in wishing Craig a very happy birthday today!
STORE: The local convenience store has been the backbone of Canadian communities for generations. In fact, our convenience store roots can be traced back to Quebec in the 1600s when Samuel de Champlain founded the first store outside of Quebec City. The more than 22,500 stores across Canada act as gathering places in many communities. Those community hubs generate more than $54 billion in sales, employ more than 200,000 Canadians and sell everything from fuel, EV charging, to lottery, energy drinks, bottled water, salty snacks and in Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, beer. Find out more about Canada’s convenience industry from its chief advocate, The Convenience Industry Council of Canada at [convenienceindustry.ca](https://convenienceindustry.ca/).
STORY: Winterlude 2026’s [Lantern Grove](https://www.lanterngrove.ca/) transforms Confederation Park into a magical, light-filled story-driven experience built around a winter tale of community and generosity. Produced by Immersive International and presented by [Ottawa Tourism](https://ottawatourism.ca/en/event-calendar/lantern-grove), visitors can wander among sculptural installations, dynamic lighting, whimsical sound design, and the enchanting Cinema Forest. A short film expands the story on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday evenings, making Lantern Grove feel like stepping inside a living Canadian winter story.
STOUT: Happy [Canadian Beer Day](https://canadianbeerday.ca/)! During the early period of Canada’s brewing history, heavier ales, porters and stouts were the more popular brews, owing to the traditional preferences of the English, Irish, Welsh and Scottish immigrants who comprised an increasing proportion of Canada’s population following the takeover of New France by Britain in 1763.
STRAW: Nothing says summer in Canada like a basket of fresh-picked strawberries! From coast to coast, strawberry season typically runs from late June to early July, with local farms offering juicy, sun-ripened berries perfect for jams, shortcakes, or snacking straight from the patch. In 2024, Canadian farmers harvested nearly 26,000 tonnes of fresh strawberries – the biggest crop in five years. Quebec leads the berry pack, producing over two-thirds of the country’s supply. Talk about a sweet success!
STRIP: Did you know that Canada has a rich history of producing iconic comic strips? One of the most famous Canadian comic strips is '[For Better or For Worse](https://fbofw.com/)' created by Lynn Johnston. This heartwarming comic strip, which debuted in 1979, follows the daily lives of the Patterson family and addresses relatable themes such as family dynamics, relationships, and social issues. 'For Better or For Worse' became widely syndicated and beloved by readers around the world, earning numerous awards and accolades for its authenticity and humour.
STYLE: Style in Canada is as diverse as the country itself – from cozy winter layers to cutting-edge couture. Canada’s fashion scene celebrates creativity and identity, with Montréal’s vibrant design houses and [Toronto’s Fashion Week](https://fashionarttoronto.ca/) runways leading the way. Brands like [Canada Goose](https://www.canadagoose.com/ca/en/home-page), [Smythe](https://shopsmythe.com/), and Indigenous-owned labels such as [Lesley Hampton](https://lesleyhampton.com/) and [Section 35](https://www.sectionthirtyfive.com/) show how Canadian style blends function, culture, and artistry – proof that true northern style never goes out of fashion!
SUITE: [Honeymoon Suite](https://honeymoonsuiteband.com/) is a Canadian rock band that was formed in 1981 in Niagara Falls, Ontario. The band's name was inspired by the fact that Niagara Falls is the unofficial honeymoon capital of the world. Honeymoon Suite won the Juno Award for Group of the Year in 1986.
SUPRA: [FC Supra du Québec](https://www.cplsoccer.com/fcsupra) is set to take the pitch in 2026 as the Canadian Premier League’s newest club, bringing top-flight pro soccer to Laval. The team will play out of Stade Boréale and is focused on developing homegrown talent, creating a pathway for Québec players to compete on a national stage. With a name that evokes rising above, FC Supra is ready to elevate the game in La Belle Province.
SWATH: A swath is the strip of crops cut by a scythe or combine – and it’s a familiar sight across Canada’s prairies. During harvest season, golden swaths of wheat and canola stretch for kilometres across provinces like Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba, painting the landscape with the colours of Canada’s breadbasket.
SWEAT: Sweat lodges are sacred spaces used by many First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities for ceremony, healing, and spiritual renewal. Inside the lodge, steam rises as water is poured over heated stones, creating an intense sweat that symbolizes purification and connection to the land, ancestors, and community. These ceremonies have been passed down for generations, offering a powerful way to reflect, give thanks, and restore balance.
SWIMS: Canada is a nation that swims! Canada's Olympic swimmers have truly made a splash on the world stage! [Canadian swimming](https://www.swimming.ca/) stars have dazzled with their impressive performances at the 2024 Paris Olympics, including [Summer McIntosh](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/summer-mcintosh/) who won three gold medals and a silver, setting new Olympic records in both the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley. [Penny Oleksiak](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/penny-oleksiak/) won a remarkable four medals at the Rio 2016 Olympics, including a gold in the 100m freestyle. [Maggie Mac Neil](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/margaret-mac-neil/) won gold in the 100m butterfly at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and [Mark Tewksbury](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/mark-tewksbury/) brought home gold in the 100m backstroke from the 1992 Barcelona Games. At the Los Angeles 1984 Olympics, Canada won 10 medals in swimming, including gold medal performances by [Alex Baumann](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/alex-baumann/), [Victor Davis](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/victor-davis/), and [Anne Ottenbrite](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/anne-ottenbrite-muylaert/). With such remarkable achievements, it's clear that Canada not only swims but excels at it!
SWINE: Canada is one of the top producers of pork in the world, with millions of pigs raised across the country, especially in provinces like Quebec, Ontario, and Manitoba. Canadian pork is a popular export, found on dinner tables across the globe! On Super Bowl Sunday, pigs make an appearance in more ways than one! While you’re enjoying pulled pork sliders or crispy bacon, it's interesting to note that the term "pigskin" for footballs originates from the early days of the sport. Originally, footballs were made from inflated pig bladders, which served as the ball's core. These bladders were encased in leather to form the ball. This "pigskin" ball was standard for football for many years before modern synthetic materials took over.
SWING: [Oscar Peterson](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/oscar-peterson) is one of Canada's most honoured musicians and is widely regarded as one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. Born and raised in Montreal, Peterson began playing piano at the age of five. Known as the "master of swing" or the "king of inside swing," Peterson made a name for himself with his incredible dexterity, speed and ornate technique on the keys. Over the course of Peterson’s acclaimed career, he won seven Grammy Awards, was awarded the Order of Canada and the Order of Ontario, won the Martin Luther King Jr. Achievement Award, received numerous honorary degrees, and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame. A public statue of Oscar Peterson was unveiled by Queen Elizabeth II in Ottawa in 2007. Check out this [Heritage Minutes video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7cdXEhR9dd4) that recounts the early years of Peterson’s music career.
SWISH: Basketball fans know the satisfying sound of a perfect shot aka the "swish," but did you know that basketball itself was invented by a Canadian? In 1891, Dr. James Naismith from Almonte, Ontario, created the game, and over a century later, Canada continues to be a major part of basketball's story. As the NBA season tips off today, the Toronto Raptors and fans across the country celebrate the legacy of Naismith's invention. From amateur courts to the pros, every swish is a tribute to Canada’s hoop heritage!
TABLE: Arguably Canada's most famous piece of furniture, Canada's historic Confederation Table is on display in the Saskatchewan Legislative Library Reading Room in Regina. The table was believed to be from the 1864 Quebec Conference where the Fathers of Confederation wrote the British North America Act, creating Canada as a country. The Confederation Table is a golden-hued oak and basswood library or refectory table constructed circa 1837 to 1864 in a Victorian Gothic Revival style.
TACKS: The [Tacks hockey skate](https://ca.ccmhockey.com/en/Skates/Shop-All-Skates/Tacks-Skates) has deep Canadian roots! It all started with George Tackaberry, a Manitoba shoemaker who crafted a better-fitting, more durable skate for professional players in the early 1900s. His design became so popular that CCM (Canada Cycle and Motor Company) took over production, making Tacks their signature hockey skate for decades. Though the brand was retired in 2006, it made a comeback in 2014, proving that a great Canadian innovation never stays on the bench for long!
TAILS: Today marks the start of [Winterlude](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/winterlude.html), the annual winter festival in Ottawa-Gatineau featuring ice, snow, and BeaverTails! [BeaverTails](https://beavertails.com/about-beavertails-pastries/) are world famous Canadian fried dough pastries that are individually stretched to resemble beaver's tails, with sweet toppings like cinnamon & sugar, chocolate hazelnut, and maple spread. They are the ultimate way to keep warm during Winterlude!
TEACH: Today is World Teachers' Day! Celebrated annually on October 5th, this day celebrates the incredible role that teachers play all over the world and their important contribution to society. In Canada, there are over 400,000 full-time and part-time educators in public elementary and secondary schools. Thank a teacher today for everything they do!
TENOR: [The Tenors](https://www.tenorsmusic.com/) (formerly known as The Canadian Tenors) are a vocal group consisting of Victor Micallef, Clifton Murray, Alberto Urso, and Mark Masri. They sing operatic pop music and have performed on more than 60 international television programs, including the Oprah Winfrey Show and the Emmy Awards. They sang at the 2009 and 2016 Grey Cup, the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, and the 2017 Invictus Games in Toronto, and won a Juno Award in 2013 for Adult Contemporary Album of the Year.
TENTH: Newfoundland and Labrador became Canada’s tenth province on March 31, 1949, following a historic vote to join Confederation. Originally known simply as Newfoundland, the province was officially renamed Newfoundland and Labrador in 2001 to better reflect its mainland territory. From colourful coastal towns to rugged northern landscapes, it’s a uniquely vibrant part of Canada’s story – tenth to join, but first in East Coast charm!
TENTS: Camping is a cherished Canadian tradition, with tents set up each summer in provincial and national parks from coast to coast to coast. From lakeside campgrounds to remote backcountry sites, Canadians head outdoors to paddle, hike, and sleep under the stars. Pitching a tent is one of the simplest ways many people connect with Canada’s vast natural landscapes and seasonal wilderness culture.
TERRY: While 'terry' can refer to a type of soft, absorbent fabric, it also carries special meaning in Canada as the name of Terry Fox, a true Canadian hero whose Marathon of Hope continues to inspire millions. In 1980, Terry set out to run across Canada to raise money for cancer research after losing his leg to the disease. Although he was forced to stop early, his legacy lives on through the annual [Terry Fox Run](https://terryfox.org/terry-fox-run/), held every September, including this year on September 15. So, when you think of Terry, remember the determination and courage that have united Canadians from coast to coast in support of a great cause!
THANK: Today we are celebrating Canuckle #1500! Reaching this milestone was a moment to pause and thank the community that has made 1500 daily puzzles possible. From coast to coast to coast, and around the world, Canuckle has become a shared part of many people’s daily routine – a quick challenge, a few guesses, and a lot of connection along the way. We’re incredibly grateful to everyone who has played, shared, and supported the game since day one. Thank you!
THING: [The Nature of Things](https://www.cbc.ca/natureofthings/) is television’s longest-running science series that debuted on CBC on November 6, 1960. It evolved into an hour-long documentary during renowned Canadian scientist and environmental activist David Suzuki’s tenure as host (1979–2023). The groundbreaking program was among the first to present scientific findings on subjects such as HIV/AIDS and climate change. Over the course of more than 60 seasons and over 900 episodes, The Nature of Things has been seen in more than 80 countries. It has received 17 Gemini Awards and seven Canadian Screen Awards.
THIRD: In curling, the third is the player who throws the third pair of stones and helps the skip plan strategy. At the 2026 Winter Olympics, Team Canada’s thirds [Marc Kennedy](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/marc-kennedy/) and [Tracy Fleury](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/tracy-fleury/) play a crucial role in every end, delivering precise shots, calling key plays, and helping their teams chase medals on the world stage. Their decisions on the ice can change the course of an entire match.
THORN: Canada has a deep-rooted love for roses, particularly the hardy Canadian Explorer rose series, developed to withstand cold winters. The [Canadian Rose Society](https://canadianrosesociety.org/), founded in 1946, promotes the appreciation and cultivation of roses across the country. Thorny roses are celebrated at the annual "Festival of Roses" held at Montréal Botanical Garden, which showcases hundreds of beautiful rose varieties. While roses have their thorns, they are a symbol of perseverance and beauty, much like the spirit of Canadian gardeners who cultivate them in challenging climates.
THRIP: [Thrips](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/thrips) are tiny, slender insects found across Canada that can cause big problems for farmers and gardeners. While many species are harmless, pests like Western Flower Thrips and Onion Thrips feed on plants and can damage crops, greenhouse vegetables, and ornamental flowers. These tiny insects may be small, but they can have a big impact on Canadian agriculture.
THRUM: In Canada, thrums are the soft wool bits knit inside thrummed mittens to keep hands extra warm in the coldest winters. This cozy technique, believed to have originated from Indigenous and Newfoundland knitting traditions, creates a fluffy lining that traps heat – perfect for those chilly Canadian days! Whether you’re outside skating or shoveling snow, thrummed mittens are a true winter essential.
TIMBER: Timber is at the heart of one of Canada’s oldest and most important industries. Canada’s vast forests produce world-class timber used in construction, furniture, and paper products worldwide. From the towering pines of British Columbia to the hardwood forests of Ontario and Quebec, different regions supply wood suited for everything from framing lumber to fine cabinetry, with sustainable management helping support communities and ecosystems for generations.
TOMBS: Across Canada, historic tombs and cemeteries take on an eerie charm each Halloween. From Montreal’s Mount Royal Cemetery to Halifax’s Old Burying Ground, some of the country’s oldest tombs date back centuries - resting places that tell stories of settlers, sailors, and soldiers. Many offer lantern-lit tours in October, blending history and haunting in true Canadian fashion.
TOOLS: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! Across Canada, tools are a familiar part of garages, workshops, and weekend projects – because if something breaks, there’s a good chance a dad has already said, “I’ve got just the tool for that!” For many, they’ve also been part of passing down practical skills, problem-solving, and hands-on learning from one generation to the next. On Father's Day we’re celebrating all the dads and father figures across the country for everything they build, fix, and figure out along the way.
TOONIE: Canada’s two-dollar coin, affectionately called the “toonie,” was introduced in 1996 to replace the $2 bill. It features an adult polar bear, designed by Ontario wildlife artist Brent Townsend, standing on an Arctic ice floe. Its name comes from a playful mix of “two” and “loonie,” the one-dollar coin. In 2002, a giant toonie statue was unveiled in Campbellford, Ontario, honouring one of the country’s most recognizable coins.
TOPAZ: Hidden beneath Canada's rugged landscapes, topaz can be found glimmering across the country, including in Bancroft, Ontario - Canada's 'Mineral Capital' - as well as in Mont Saint-Hilaire, Quebec, and in British Columbia's abundant felsic plutonic rocks. This brilliant gemstone forms in granite pegmatites and can dazzle in shades of yellow and rich golden brown! Though Canada isn't a major source of gem-quality topaz, rockhounds cherish the stunning specimens unearthed in these geological hotspots.
TOTAL: On April 8, 2024, a spectacular and rare celestial event is set to unfold over Canada, the United States and Mexico – a [total solar eclipse](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronomy/eclipses/total-solar-eclipse.asp). As the Moon aligns perfectly between Earth and the Sun, temporary darkness will sweep across parts of the country, captivating countless spectators. In Canada, the solar eclipse's path of totality will pass through some cities and towns in Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, plunging them into darkness for a few minutes. People outside the path of totality will be able to observe a partial solar eclipse, during which the Sun is not hidden in totality.
TOTEM: The word totem comes from the Algonquian word “odoodem“ meaning “his kinship group“.
TOURS: World Tourism Day, created by the United Nations World Tourism Organization, is celebrated each year on September 27th to spread awareness about the importance of tourism and its impact on our society. Canada is a country filled with famous landmarks, historical wonders, delicious food, incredible culture, and all the outdoor exploration you could want. Whether you are touring the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, touring one of Canada's many national parks and historic sites, touring Niagara Falls, or taking a tour through the Canadian Rockies, there are so many natural and cultural wonders to enjoy in our country!
TOXIC: During the First World War, a Canadian innovation helped protect soldiers from toxic gases on the battlefield. The [Hypo Helmet](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/hypo-helmet), invented by Newfoundland doctor Captain Cluny Macpherson in 1915, was an early type of gas mask designed to filter out toxic gases like chlorine gas. It was made of a chemically treated flannel hood with a mica visor, and was a crucial development in protecting soldiers from the harmful effects of chemical warfare. This Canadian invention was an important step in the evolution of gas masks, helping to save countless lives during the war.
TRACE: [Leave No Trace Canada](https://leavenotrace.ca/) is a non-profit organization dedicated to promoting outdoor ethics and the seven Leave No Trace principles with the goal of encouraging Canadians to enjoy the benefits of the outdoors while protecting Canada's natural and cultural heritage. The mission of Leave No Trace Canada is to promote and inspire responsible outdoor recreation through science-based education and partnerships throughout Canada.
TRACK: Canada's best summer Olympic sport is athletics, which includes running, hurdles, long jump, high jump, decathlon and other track & field events. Canada has earned 66 medals in athletics since 1900, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 33 bronze.
TRADE: Canada’s three biggest trading partners are the United States, the European Union and China. Goods and services trade with the US totaled over $800 billion in 2021.
TRAIL: The [Trans Canada Trail](https://tctrail.ca/) is Canada’s national trail and is the longest network of multi-use recreational trails in the world. Crossing Canada on the Trans Canada Trail by foot would take over two years, spanning a whopping 24,134 km!
TRAPS: For generations, traps have played an important role in Canada’s wilderness heritage. From beaver pelts that helped build early trade to modern wildlife management, trapping has shaped both communities and the landscape. Today, [National Hunting, Trapping and Fishing Heritage Day](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/annualstatutes/2014_26/FullText.html) celebrates this part of Canada’s history, honouring the skills and traditions that connect people to the great outdoors.
TRAWL: Dragging large fishing nets through the water, a method known as trawling, is widely used in Canadian fisheries along both coasts. From the Atlantic provinces to British Columbia, trawling supports important commercial fishing communities and contributes significantly to Canada’s seafood industry. But it’s not just about catching fish – sustainable trawling practices are essential for protecting marine ecosystems, helping ensure these waters remain rich and vibrant for generations to come.
TRIKE: Aqua trikes are making waves across Canada! These big-wheeled, pedal-powered water tricycles let riders glide across lakes and ponds with ease - a fun, stable ride that’s popular with families and adventurers alike. You can find them in Collingwood, Ontario, Cardigan, Prince Edward Island, and Kelowna, British Columbia, just to name a few. Aqua Trikes give Canadians of all ages a playful, unique way to enjoy the water and the outdoors.
TRUTH: Truth is one of The Seven Grandfather Teachings which are a set of Anishinaabe guiding principles that give people the tools for how to live a good life. They have been passed down from generation to generation for thousands of years through stories and ceremonies. Truth is represented by the turtle, who was here during the creation of Earth and carries all of life’s teachings on his back.
TULIP: The Canadian Tulip Festival in Ottawa features 100 tulip varieties with more than one million blooms over 14,000 m². The celebration is a symbol of friendship between Canada and the Netherlands, with 20,000 bulbs being gifted by the Netherlands each year.
TWEED: [Tweed, Ontario](https://tweed.ca/) is packed with small-town charm, from North America’s smallest jailhouse to its brightly painted fire hydrants inspired by a Pakistan–Ontario exchange program hosted by Canada World Youth in 1987. The community sits along the Moira River near Stoco Lake, making it a favourite fishing spot — especially for muskie and crappie. Each summer, the town also hosts the Tweed Stampede, Ontario’s largest rodeo, celebrating country music, family fun, and community spirit.
TWICE: April 11th is National Poutine Day, and what better way to enjoy this iconic Canadian dish than with twice-fried potatoes! Most traditional poutine recipes call for the potatoes to be fried twice, creating that perfect balance of crispy on the outside and soft on the inside. This ensures the fries can hold up to the rich gravy and squeaky cheese curds without getting soggy. Whether you stick with the classic or get creative, twice-fried fries are the key to the ultimate poutine experience!
TWINS: The Edison Twins is a Canadian children's television program which ran for six seasons on CBC Television from March 3, 1984 to December 17, 1986. The series featured the adventures of Tom and Annie Edison (played by Andrew Sabiston and Marnie McPhail respectively), a pair of teenage scientific prodigy siblings who face a variety of challenges which they overcome with their expertise of science. McPhail won the Gemini Award for Best Performance by a Lead Actress in a Continuing Dramatic Series in 1986.
UDDER: Cows are at the heart of the [Canadian dairy industry](https://dairyfarmersofcanada.ca/), which produces everything from milk and butter to cheese and yogurt. Milk is collected from the udder, the part of the cow where it's stored before being carefully cooled and transported. Canada is home to over 10,000 dairy farms, and its farmers follow some of the highest standards in the world for quality, safety, and animal care. So the next time you pour a glass of milk or bite into a gooey grilled cheese, you can thank a Canadian cow!
UMAMI: Umami, known as the “fifth flavour”, is all about rich, savoury taste, and Canada has plenty to offer! From the smoky depth of maple-glazed bacon to the bold bite of aged cheddar and wild mushrooms, Canadian cuisine is packed with umami-rich flavours. Whether it’s a comforting plate of poutine with hearty gravy or a delicious tourtière, these tastes prove Canada knows how to bring savoury satisfaction to the table.
URINE: Canadian researchers recently made a splash by helping design a urinal that virtually eliminates splashback! University of Waterloo professor Zhao Pan and PhD student Kaveeshan Thurairajah were part of the team awarded the [2026 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics](https://uwaterloo.ca/mechanical-mechatronics-engineering/news/mme-researchers-recognized-ig-nobel-physics-prize-innovative) for the work. Their research found that keeping the angle where a urine stream hits the urinal below about 30 degrees dramatically reduces splashing, inspiring a new design called the Nautilus, which the researchers dubbed the “Nauti-Loo.”
USHER: The [Usher of the Black Rod](https://sencanada.ca/en/about/usher-black-rod) is a key figure in Canada’s Parliament! This official serves as the personal attendant of the Monarch and the Governor General and is responsible for summoning Members of Parliament to the Senate Chamber during the Speech from the Throne and the opening of Parliament. The role dates back centuries and symbolizes the connection between the Senate and the House of Commons. The Black Rod itself is a ceremonial staff, representing the Usher's authority - one of the many traditions that shape Canada's government!
VAULT: [Qaumajuq](https://www.wag.ca/about/qaumajuq/) is an innovative new museum in Winnipeg, Manitoba, home of the largest public collection of contemporary Inuit art in the world. The first thing you’ll see when you step inside Qaumajuq is the stunning, three-storey glass vault filled with thousands of Inuit carvings. The [Visible Vault](https://vault.wag.ca/) provides unprecedented access to close to 5,000 Inuit stone carvings, providing a unique, immersive art-viewing experience. It is the world's only visible vault of its kind.
VISIT: The first official Royal Visit to Canada was in 1860, when Prince Albert Edward (later King Edward VII) toured the country. Since then, members of the Royal Family have made dozens of visits, strengthening ties between Canada and the Crown. Queen Elizabeth II visited Canada 22 times during her reign – more than any other Commonwealth nation! Most recently, [King Charles III visited Canada in May 2025](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/2025-royal-visit.html), becoming only the second reigning monarch to deliver Canada's Speech from the Throne.
VISTA: Canada’s stunning scenery and mind-defying vistas are a well-known draw to the country. Rugged mountain ranges, thundering rivers and turquoise lakes surrounded by alpine forests – Canada is an absolute wonder to behold! From sweeping grasslands to crashing ocean tides to craggy snow-covered mountains, Canada’s diverse landscapes offer awe-inspiring vistas for every taste.
WAFER: Yesterday was World Chocolate Day! The popular Canadian chocolate bar, "Coffee Crisp," features layers of vanilla wafer and coffee-flavoured cream covered in milk chocolate. It's a unique Canadian treat, and it rarely ventures beyond Canada's borders. The candy has largely been made exclusively for Canadian markets - over 150 million Coffee Crisp bars are produced every year in the Nestlé Canada factory in Toronto. How do Canadians like their coffee? Crisp!
WAGON: The [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/) starts today! One of its most iconic events is the chuckwagon race, where teams of horses and drivers compete in a high-speed tribute to the wagons that once carried supplies across the Prairies. First introduced in 1923, chuckwagon racing has become a fan-favourite tradition – blending Western heritage, rodeo spirit, and heart-pounding excitement at “The Greatest Outdoor Show on Earth!”
WATER: With around 80,423 cubic metres per capita, Canada has about 9% of the world's total renewable fresh water supply. When glacier, underground and lake water is included, Canada actually has 20% of the world's fresh water supply.
WAXER: The Markham Waxers were an Ontario Junior Hockey League (OJHL) Junior "A" ice hockey team based in Markham, Ontario. Originally known as the Markham Jets, the Waxers organization changed names in 1961, named after The International Group, a privately owned wax and oil refinery that originated in Agincourt, Ontario. At one point, the Waxers were the farm team of the National Hockey League's Toronto Maple Leafs and boasts over 100 NHL and World Hockey Association graduates. The Waxers name is still used by the [Markham Waxers](https://waxers.com/) minor hockey club.
WEAVE: There are an estimated 7,000 or 8,000 weavers in Ontario, Québec and British Columbia, and weavers' guilds exist in most large communities in Canada. Over thousands of years, Indigenous peoples of North America perfected the art of basket weaving. Weavers manipulated grasses, bark, roots, and other plant materials into baskets that served a variety of functions. The Salish peoples of the Northwest Coast have had a long history of weaving and textile manufacture, using mountain-goat hair, fireweed and woolly dog hair.
WEDGE: The Gooderham Building, also known as the Flatiron Building, is an historic office building at 49 Wellington Street East in Toronto, Ontario. Built in 1891 to the designs of architect David Roberts Jr., it is an iconic historical structure in the heart of the provincial capital. Its wedge-like shape and distinctive colours are probably why it is one of the most photographed structures in the city!
WHALE: There are more than 33 species of whale that live in Canada's oceans.
WHELK: Whelks are spiral-shelled sea snails commonly found in the cold waters off Canada's Atlantic coast. These hardy creatures are not only a key part of marine ecosystems but also an important catch in the fishing industry, where they are harvested for their delicate meat and exported worldwide. Indigenous peoples have long valued whelks, using their shells to create tools, jewellery, and even decorative wampum beads. These small but mighty molluscs are a fascinating part of Canada's coastal heritage!
WIRED: Canada's early internet networks relied on being wired to telephone lines and later advanced to fibre optics, connecting the nation's vast geography. In 1984, NetNorth, Canada's first digital network, linked universities using dial-up lines, allowing researchers to exchange data across provinces. This wired system laid the foundation for CA*net in 1990, Canada's first national internet backbone, which revolutionized communication and collaboration across the country. From these humble beginnings, Canada's internet infrastructure has grown into one of the most advanced in the world!
WOODS: Canada is famously covered in vast woods – with nearly 40% of the country blanketed by forests, making it one of the world’s greenest nations. These woods are home to countless species and provide endless opportunities for outdoor adventures. Since 1926, the Canadian company [Woods](https://www.woods.ca/) has been a trusted name for camping gear, helping adventurers connect with nature across these expansive woodlands. Whether exploring or camping, the woods are truly at the heart of Canada’s great outdoors!
WOVEN: Today is [Red Dress Day](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/red-dress-day) in Canada – a day to honour and remember Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women, Girls, and Two-Spirit People (MMIWG2S). The red dresses hanging in windows and trees across the country serve as powerful symbols of those whose lives have been taken and those still missing. Traditional Indigenous clothing is often woven with deep cultural meaning, with intricate designs and patterns that reflect stories, spiritual beliefs, and connections to the land. These garments are more than just clothing – they are a form of storytelling, passed down through generations. On Red Dress Day, the red dresses themselves are a modern reflection of these woven traditions, symbolizing strength, resilience, and the ongoing call for justice.
WRECK: Named as one of the best Gordon Lightfoot songs of all time, "The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald" tells the real-life story of the Edmund Fitzgerald, an ore carrier that sank in Lake Superior in 1975 and took 29 nine members of the crew with it. Beautifully arranged, and blessed with some truly stupendous lyrics, it remains one of his most poignant and popular songs. Released just one year after the disaster, it sailed to No. 1 in Canada and No. 2 on the US Billboard Hot 100. Gordon Lightfoot was a Canadian singer-songwriter and guitarist who achieved international success in folk, folk-rock, and country music. He is credited with helping to define the folk-pop sound of the 1960s and 1970s. He has been referred to as Canada's greatest songwriter and was known internationally as a folk-rock legend. #RIPGordonLightfoot
WRIST: [Ringette](https://www.ringette.ca/), invented in 1963 by Canadian Sam Jacks, is a fast-paced ice sport where players use straight sticks to control a rubber ring. The wrist shot is the most common way to score, making quick wrist movements and precise passes the heart of this uniquely Canadian game. From backyard rinks to national arenas, every goal begins with a flick of the wrist! Canuckle is excited to be sponsoring the U12A Nepean Ravens Beswick ringette team this season!
YAHOO: The [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/) starts today! Did you know that "Yahoo!" is a spirited shout famously associated with the Stampede? This annual rodeo and exhibition, held every July in Calgary, Alberta, is one of Canada's largest and most famous events. During the Stampede, "Yahoo!" becomes a rallying cry for excitement and celebration, heard from cowboys, cowgirls, and spectators alike. The Stampede features thrilling rodeo events, chuckwagon races, parades, and concerts, drawing visitors from all over the world. The enthusiastic "Yahoo!" shout encapsulates the vibrant and festive spirit of this iconic Canadian event. The official Stampede mascot, Harry the Horse has been saying "Yahoo!" since he debuted with his bell and signs on March 14, 1985.
YARDS: It's Grey Cup Sunday! In Canadian football, the game revolves around gaining those all-important yards - and in Canada there is more ground to cover! The CFL field is 110 yards long, compared to the NFL's 100 yards, making each play a battle for just a bit more space. Fans across Canada will be cheering as teams charge down the field, fighting for every yard at the [111th Grey Cup in Vancouver](https://www.cfl.ca/category/111th-grey-cup/). Whether it's a sprint to the end zone or a nail-biting finish, Canada’s love for the game is about heart, hustle, and those extra few yards that make all the difference!
